cards.title: THE KITCHEN
cards.tagline: SEVEN ZONES. START AT THE SINK.
cards.objective: The kitchen is seven small places, not one big job. This card is the map and the order.
zones_in_order: KZ-005 Lower Cabinet and Cookware Zone
cards.start_here: KZ-003 Sink and Dishwashing Zone. It is the shortest zone, it is the point the whole kitchen resets from, and you will have finished something in fifteen minutes.
how_to_play: 1. Deal the seven ZONE cards face up. Pick the one that is annoying you today, or take the one this card says to start at.
2. Lay out that zone's three FRICTION cards. Keep the ones that are true in your kitchen. Put the rest back.
3. Turn a friction card over and pick the answer that is true. It names a ROOT CAUSE.
4. The root cause card names the ACTION cards that fix that cause. Pick the one that matches the time you actually have: five, fifteen or thirty minutes.
5. Do it standing up, with the card in your hand.
6. Read the victory condition out loud. If it is not true yet, you are not finished, and that is the whole scoring system.
7. Fill in the zone's STANDARD card with a pen and put it where the zone is.
8. Draw an EVENT card when an ordinary hard day happens, and see whether the standard held.
cards.players: 1 to 6. With more than one, deal the friction cards out and let each person keep the ones they believe. Disagreement is the useful part, not a problem to resolve before starting.
cards.six_s: Sort, Straighten, Shine, Safety, Standardize, Sustain
cards.safety_first: Do KA-016 The Hot Zone Walk before any rebuild. It takes fifteen minutes and the rebuilds move heavy and sharp things around.

cards.title: PRIMARY PREP COUNTER
cards.tagline: ONE CLEAR RUN. THE REST GOES SOMEWHERE ELSE.
cards.objective: The stretch of counter where food is actually cut, mixed, and plated.
callouts: Clear run, at least as wide as your largest cutting board
The cutting board, down on bare counter
Knife block or wall strip, on your dominant side
Salt within one reach
Kettle and toaster back against the wall, cords coiled
Nothing parked: no mail, no fruit bowl, no charging phone
cards.done_looks_like: One clear run of counter at least as wide as your largest cutting board, holding only the board, the knife block or strip, and the salt. The kettle and the toaster stand back against the wall with their cords coiled, and there is no mail, no fruit bowl, and no charging phone anywhere on the surface.

safety_checks.question: Fall, cut, or crush
safety_checks.text: A chef's knife left blade-up in the drying rack, or slid under suds in a full sink, is the most common serious cut in a home kitchen.

safety_checks.question: Burn or fire
safety_checks.text: A toaster pushed under a low cabinet or against a paper towel roll puts heat and flame right where nothing can escape it.

the_call.title: The stand mixer question
the_call.text: The hard one is the appliance you genuinely love and rarely use: the mixer, the bread machine, the espresso setup. Count real uses over the past month, not the ones you intended. Anything you reach for less than a couple of times a week comes off the counter and goes to a low cabinet, ideally on a pull-out. Anything you have not switched on in a year leaves the kitchen entirely. And if your honest reason for keeping it out is that lifting it from a cabinet would stop you using it, you have just proved the machine is not part of your cooking, and it is worth more sold than stored.

safety_checks.question: Burn or fire
safety_checks.text: Oil left heating unattended, and a tea towel or a paper roll stored within reach of a live burner, are the two ways a kitchen fire actually starts.

safety_checks.question: Fall, cut, or crush
safety_checks.text: A pan handle turned out over the front edge of the hob is at exactly the height a toddler grabs, and it comes down with the contents.

the_call.title: The spice rack you are not honest about
the_call.text: Every cook keeps jars bought for one recipe from one holiday. Open them and smell them, one by one, over the bin. Ground spices fade first, and if a jar smells of dust rather than of itself, it is no longer seasoning anything you cook, and keeping it does not recover what you paid. Then make the harder call underneath: keep spices for the food you cooked in the last year, not the food you imagine cooking. If you want that cuisine back, buy the two spices fresh on the day you cook it. A rack you can read is worth more than a rack that is complete.

cards.title: SINK AND DISHWASHING ZONE
cards.tagline: THE WHOLE KITCHEN RESETS FROM HERE.
cards.objective: The washing point for dishes, hands, and produce, and the place the whole kitchen resets from.
callouts: Empty sink, dry basin
Drain flange wiped
One brush and one sponge standing where they drain
Drying rack empty, or holding only what is still wet
Under the sink: one tray, dish soap, tablets, one cleaner
Pipes visible around the tray
cards.done_looks_like: An empty sink with a dry basin and a wiped drain flange. One brush and one sponge standing upright where they drain rather than lying in a puddle. The drying rack either empty or holding only what is still wet. Under the sink, a single tray holding dish soap, dishwasher tablets, and one all-purpose cleaner, with the pipes visible around them.

safety_checks.question: Water and electricity
safety_checks.text: A kettle, a socket, or a charging phone within splash distance of the basin, handled with wet hands, is the electrical risk this room actually has.

safety_checks.question: Poison, choke, or strangle
safety_checks.text: Bleach mixed with an acidic or ammonia cleaner in the basin releases a gas that will drive you out of the room, and both bottles usually live under this sink.

the_call.title: Whether soaking is allowed
the_call.text: The real decision in this zone is not what to keep, it is whether you let the basin be a staging area. Soaking is the word a kitchen uses for postponing, and one soaking pan gives every other dish permission to join it. Settle it with a deadline rather than a ban: a pan may soak, but only until the current dishwasher cycle ends or until you next leave the room, whichever comes first. If a dish cannot meet that deadline, it gets washed now or goes in the machine dirty. The rule holds because it names a moment, and moments arrive on their own.

safety_checks.question: Fall, cut, or crush
safety_checks.text: Glassware stacked at or above head height fails onto a hard floor and onto whoever opened the door.

safety_checks.question: Fall
safety_checks.text: Reaching the top shelf from a chair, a counter edge, or an open drawer is how people fall in kitchens, and it happens while holding something breakable.

the_call.title: The second set of dishes
the_call.text: Almost every kitchen holds two sets: the one you eat off and the good one, or the one from before you moved. Pick one everyday set, sized to the people who eat here plus two, and give it the shelf between shoulder and eye height. Then decide the second set honestly. If it has not been on a table in two years and nobody has asked to inherit it, it goes now, whole, to somewhere it will be used. If it is genuinely somebody's grandmother's, sentiment gets to keep the objects but does not get to keep the shelf you reach into daily: box it, label it, and store it outside the kitchen. What you cannot do is keep both sets at eye level and then blame the cabinet for being full.

Pans nested no more than three deep or stood on edge in a divider, lids in a rack or on a door rail instead of loose, baking sheets standing on end, and the two pans you cook with nightly at the front of the cabinet nearest the hob. Nothing has to come out to reach anything else.

safety_checks.question: Fall, cut, or crush
safety_checks.text: A tall nest of pans or a cast iron pot stored above waist height comes down on hands and feet the moment the stack shifts.

safety_checks.question: Fall, cut, or crush
safety_checks.text: Food processor and blender blades stored loose inside a bowl in a low cabinet are found by fingers reaching into the dark.

the_call.title: The third frying pan
the_call.text: Cook a normal week and count the most pans you had going at once. That number plus one is your cap, and everything beyond it goes, including the expensive one you never liked using. The money is already spent, and keeping the pan does not get any of it back; it only costs you the low shelf. Then handle the guest argument separately: if a piece earns its place twice a year for visitors, and a roasting tray you already own could do the same job, keep the tray and release the piece. A cookware set kept for a hypothetical dinner party takes up the easiest shelf in the kitchen every day of the year for two evenings of use.

safety_checks.question: Fall, cut, or crush
safety_checks.text: An unsheathed mandoline blade or paring knife lying loose among the spatulas cuts the hand that goes in looking for something else.

safety_checks.question: Poison, choke, or strangle
safety_checks.text: Loose button batteries rolling in a utility drawer at child height are swallowed easily and do serious internal damage fast.

the_call.title: The drawer everyone calls the junk drawer
the_call.text: A kitchen is allowed one drawer of small useful things, but it has to be a named drawer with a category and a divider, not an amnesty. Write its list: tape, string, a torch, batteries, a working pen, the takeaway menus you actually order from. Everything in there must be something you would come to the kitchen looking for. Then take an empty box, and anything you cannot name a use for while you are holding it goes in the box. Date the box, put it on a shelf, and if nothing has been pulled out of it by the end of the season it leaves unopened. The screws in the envelope and the manual for the dead printer are not kitchen items, and they are the reason the drawer no longer opens.

cards.title: REFRIGERATOR AND FREEZER
cards.tagline: SEE WHAT YOU OWN BEFORE YOU SHOP.
cards.objective: Cold storage that has to keep food safe and show you what you already own before you shop.

cards.done_looks_like: Raw meat sealed on the lowest shelf. Leftovers in clear containers at eye level, each with a name and a date on the lid. One bin marked for what must be eaten this week, sitting where the door opens straight onto it. The vents at the back wall clear of anything pressed against them, the door holding condiments only, and nothing in the freezer without a label.

safety_checks.question: Poison, choke, or strangle
safety_checks.text: Juices from a raw meat package stored above ready-to-eat food drip onto what nobody is going to cook again, and the salad is the usual victim.

safety_checks.question: Fall, cut, or crush
safety_checks.text: Heavy glass jars stored at the top of the door or on the top shelf fall onto a tiled floor when the door is swung, and they shatter at foot level.

the_call.title: The container you keep moving to the front
the_call.text: The genuinely hard call here is not the obviously spoiled food, it is the container of good leftovers you have now shifted forward three times. Ask what would actually have to happen for it to be eaten, and be concrete: which meal, which day, who eats it. If you cannot answer, it is not food you are storing, it is the guilt of having cooked too much. Bin it today, then fix the cause rather than the symptom: cook a smaller batch, or portion leftovers into a lunch container the same evening you cook, before the fridge door closes. A leftover that goes in already assigned to a meal gets eaten. A leftover that goes in undecided is a decision you have only postponed at four degrees.

cards.title: CLEAR THE RUN
cards.tagline: 15 MINUTES. 1.
cards.objective: Get one unbroken run of counter back, and prove it can hold.
cards.why_it_matters: You cannot cook in twenty centimetres, and every other habit in this kitchen starts on this surface.
inputs: the dining table, as a staging area
steps: Take everything off the prep counter and set it on the dining table. Everything, including the things you are sure belong there.
Let only three things back: what you cut on, what you cut with, and what you season with.
Lift the kettle and the toaster rather than wiping around them, clean under their feet, set them back against the wall and coil the cords.
Everything still on the table goes to a home elsewhere, or leaves. Do not put one item back to decide about later, because that is the item the pile grows from.
Wipe the run and lay the board down on bare counter.
cards.victory_condition: Your largest cutting board lies flat with room on both sides, and nothing else is on the run.

cards.title: REBUILD THE PREP COUNTER
cards.tagline: 30 MINUTES. 1 TO 2.
cards.objective: Change the counter so clear is the easy state rather than the daily effort.
cards.why_it_matters: A surface you have to defend every evening was laid out wrong. Fix the layout and the defending stops.
inputs: low tack tape or a marker
steps: Stand where you actually cut, and do not move. That spot is the anchor and everything else is measured from it.
Measure your largest board and mark that width under the counter lip with tape, so where the work surface starts is a fact and not an opinion.
Knives on your dominant side, on a wall strip or in a block. Oil and salt behind the board rather than beside it.
Mixing bowls into the cabinet directly underneath, so you can reach one without turning around.

Count real uses of every appliance still on the counter over the past month, not intended ones. Under a couple of times a week, it goes to a low cabinet. Not switched on in a year, it leaves the kitchen.
cards.victory_condition: You can cut, season, and reach a mixing bowl without taking a step or turning around.

steps: Empty the utensil crock out onto the counter.
Put back six tools, each one you actually used this month. The rest go to a drawer or leave the kitchen.
Oil, salt and pepper within one reach of the burner you use most.
Clear the landing space beside the hob down to bare counter, wide enough to set a hot pan on.
Turn every pan handle in, so nothing sticks out over the front edge.

cards.title: REBUILD THE COOKING ZONE
cards.tagline: 30 MINUTES. 1.
cards.objective: Lay the burner surround out for one reach, and take the fire risk out of it.
cards.why_it_matters: Oil left heating and a tea towel stored within reach of a live burner are the two ways a kitchen fire actually starts.
inputs: a small hook and its fixing
a food area degreaser and a microfibre cloth
steps: Mount a hook for the pot holders within a hand's reach of the burners and clear of the heat, so you never hunt for them with a hot pan.
Pull every spice jar. Anything not used in a year leaves. The ones you reach for weekly go to the front row.
Move the paper towel roll, the tea towels and any packaging off the burner side entirely.
Degrease the surround and the hob, working top down so what you loosen falls onto surfaces you have not cleaned yet.

After cleaning, light every burner once and watch for an even blue ring. A lazy yellow flame, or a burner that clicks and will not catch, is a call to a registered engineer and not a thing to adjust yourself.
cards.victory_condition: Pot holders found without looking, weekly spices in the front row, nothing that burns within reach of a burner, and every burner lighting evenly.

steps: Empty the sink completely, including the pan you were going to soak.
Wipe the basin dry, and wipe the drain flange, which is the part nobody cleans and everybody smells.
One brush and one sponge, standing where they drain. Everything else comes off the surround.
Take out of the drying rack anything that is already dry.
Wipe the tap and the surround, and dry them so no water sits.

cards.title: REBUILD UNDER THE SINK
cards.tagline: 30 MINUTES. 1.
cards.objective: One tray, the pipes visible, and nothing stored that can react with anything beside it.
cards.why_it_matters: This is the one cabinet in the house where two ordinary bottles make a gas that will drive you out of the room.
inputs: your local household chemical disposal rules
steps: Take everything out. Everything, including the bottles at the back.

Separate bleach from any acidic or ammonia based cleaner, and never store them in the same tray. If you cannot tell what a bottle is, read the label. If it has no label, dispose of it by your local rules rather than guessing.
Anything hazardous that sits within a child's reach moves up and out of this cabinet, or the cabinet gets a latch.
One shallow tray goes back, holding dish soap, dishwasher tablets and one all purpose cleaner. That is the whole inventory.
Leave the pipework visible, so a leak is something you see early instead of something you smell late.
cards.victory_condition: One tray, three bottles, and bare pipes you can see all the way around.

steps: Bring down everything you use less than once a month.
Send it to the top shelf, on its edge where it will stand.
Everything daily comes to the shelf between your shoulder and your eye.
One category per stack. Plates with plates, bowls with bowls, and nothing perched on top of a different thing.
Cap plate stacks at about six, and space the mugs so each one lifts out without moving another.

cards.title: REBUILD THE UPPER CABINETS
cards.tagline: 30 MINUTES. 1 TO 2.
cards.objective: Band the cabinet by height so nobody climbs for anything they use every day.
cards.why_it_matters: Reaching a top shelf from a chair, a counter edge or an open drawer is how people fall in kitchens, and it happens while they are holding something breakable.
inputs: a step stool with a handrail
somewhere outside the kitchen for the second set
steps: Have the shortest adult who uses this kitchen fetch the everyday plates while you watch. Their reach is the test, not yours.
Band the cabinet: below shoulder and shoulder to eye are for daily things, above eye is for monthly or less.
No glass above head height. None, in any cabinet, for any reason.
Second sets, inherited china and the platter for eight go to the top shelf or out of the kitchen altogether.
If something still needs a climb, buy a two step stool with a handrail and keep it in the kitchen. Never a chair, never a drawer edge, never the counter.

cards.title: COOKWARE RESET
cards.tagline: 15 MINUTES. 1.
cards.objective: The two pans you cook with nightly at the front, everything else capped at three deep.
cards.why_it_matters: Taking four pans out to use one is why they end up living on the floor of the kitchen.
inputs: floor space to lay everything out
steps: Take out every pan and every lid.
Put back the two you cook with nightly, at the front, in the cabinet nearest the hob.

a lid rack or a door rail
a sheathed box for loose blades
steps: Heaviest pieces onto the cabinet floor. Nothing heavy above shoulder height anywhere in this kitchen.
Set a divider or a pair of tension rods so baking sheets, boards and shallow pans stand on end.
Fit a lid rack, or a rail on the inside of the door, so no lid is ever loose.
Food processor and blender blades go into a sheathed box, never loose inside a bowl in a dark low cabinet where fingers go looking.
Test it: fetch your three most used pans one at a time and count the movements. Two or fewer, or move it again.

cards.tagline: 15 MINUTES. 1.
cards.objective: One drawer, one job, and it closes with one push.
cards.why_it_matters: A drawer with no job accepts everything, and then nothing in it can be found.
steps: One drawer at a time. Tip it out onto a tray.
Say the drawer's one job out loud before anything goes back into it.
Only that category returns. Everything else goes to the drawer it belongs in, or out of the kitchen.
Sheath every blade. If a blade has no sheath, it does not go back in until it has one.
Close it. If it does not close flush with one push, take something out rather than shoving it.

Divided insert for flatware, with nothing loose beside it.
Foil, cling film and baking paper stand on end so you can read the boxes from above.
Button batteries and anything small enough to be swallowed leave the low drawers entirely, into a lidded box stored high.
Give the junk drawer a real job, or dissolve it. Tape, batteries and a tape measure can each have a home. The rest of it is a decision you have been storing instead of making.

cards.title: FRIDGE RESET
cards.tagline: 15 MINUTES. 1.
cards.objective: Raw low, dates on, one eat first bin at the front.
cards.why_it_matters: Most food thrown away in a house was bought on purpose and then became invisible.
inputs: a neutral pH cleaner and a cloth
steps: Bin the obvious. Do not negotiate with a container you have to smell.
Raw meat down to the lowest shelf, sealed, so nothing can drip onto anything you will not cook again.
Put one shallow bin at the front of the middle shelf, where the door opens straight onto it, and put everything within three days of turning into it.
A blank label and a date on every leftover, on the lid where you will read it.
Wipe the one shelf you cleared. One shelf today is a finished job; the whole fridge is an abandoned one.

cards.title: REBUILD THE FRIDGE
cards.tagline: 30 MINUTES. 1 TO 2.
cards.objective: Assign every shelf a job, and make the cold chain visible.
cards.why_it_matters: A fridge without assigned shelves is filled by whoever unpacks the shopping, which is why the raw chicken ends up over the salad.
steps: Assign the shelves out loud and agree them with whoever else shops: raw low and sealed, leftovers at eye level, door for condiments only.
Pull anything pressed against the rear vents. Blocked vents cost cooling and they cost money every day.
Clear containers only for anything you want eaten. Opaque food is forgotten food.

Put a thermometer in and check it. The usual food safety guidance is a fridge at or below 5C or 41F and a freezer at minus 18C or 0F; if yours will not hold that, it is a repair call, not a storage problem.
Set the eat first bin where the door opens straight onto it, and nothing else goes in that spot.
cards.victory_condition: Anyone unpacking the shopping can put it away correctly without being told, and the thermometer reads in range.

cards.title: THE HOT ZONE WALK
cards.tagline: 15 MINUTES. 1, AND ONE OTHER PERSON TO DISAGREE WITH YOU.
cards.objective: Six checks across the whole kitchen, and an honest answer on each.
cards.why_it_matters: Safety outranks tidy and it outranks pretty. Do this card before any of the rebuilds, because the rebuilds move heavy and sharp things around.
cards.players: 1, and one other person to disagree with you
inputs: nothing but fifteen minutes and your eyes
steps: Blades. Every blade sheathed, in a block, or on a strip. None loose in a drawer, none blade up in a drying rack, none under suds in a full sink.
Weight. Nothing heavy above shoulder height. No glass above head height.
Heat. Tea towels, paper roll and packaging out of reach of any burner, and the toaster clear of the cabinet above it.
Water and electricity. No kettle, socket, or charging phone within splash distance of the basin.
Chemicals. Bleach stored apart from any acidic or ammonia cleaner, everything labelled, and anything hazardous out of a child's reach.
Raw above ready to eat. Nothing raw stored above anything that will not be cooked again.
cards.victory_condition: Six checks done, and you can say out loud which ones failed. Anything involving gas, a scorch mark, a frayed cord, or a burner that will not light is a call to a qualified person and not a job for this card.

cards.why_it_matters: Buying what you already own is a visibility problem, and it costs money every single month.
inputs: one list, in one place everyone can reach
steps: Before the list, open the fridge and look in the eat first bin. Write the list from what is there.
Anything down to its last one goes on the list now, not when it runs out.
One list, one place, and everyone in the house can add to it.
Put the shopping away into the fridge order you assigned, not wherever there is a gap.
Note anything you bought that you already owned. That is the measure this card improves.

cards.title: THE TWO COOK TREATY
cards.tagline: 20 MINUTES. EVERYONE WHO USES THIS KITCHEN.
cards.objective: One sentence about this kitchen that two people will both sign.
cards.why_it_matters: The dishwasher argument is not about the dishwasher. Two people are running one zone by two designs, and both of them are right.
inputs: one card each and a pen
twenty minutes when nobody is hungry
steps: Each person writes, separately and without discussion, what this kitchen should look like at bedtime. One sentence.
Read them out. Circle what you agree on. That part is already your standard.
Where you differ, name the value underneath it rather than arguing the arrangement: speed, calm, cleanliness, or being able to see things.
Design for the shared outcome and accommodate the difference. If one person needs it visible and one needs it hidden, put it visible inside a closed door.
Write the sentence you both signed onto the standard card, and put it where the disagreement actually happens.
cards.victory_condition: One sentence, two signatures, on the wall, and neither person had to lose.
